description: Black Americans, the war effort, Brown v Board 1954, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
content_html:
Black Americans and the War Effort

When the USA entered the Second World War in 1941, approximately 1 million African Americans served in the armed forces. Yet they did so in segregated units — the military operated under the same Jim Crow system of racial separation that governed life in the South. Black soldiers trained at segregated bases, were often assigned to labour rather than combat roles, and faced daily humiliations — some were refused service at lunch counters in towns near their bases while German prisoners of war were served without question.

African American civil rights leaders launched the Double V Campaign in 1942: Victory against fascism overseas and Victory against racism at home. The Pittsburgh Courier newspaper popularised the slogan. Though the campaign did not immediately change policy, it demonstrated that Black Americans' expectations had shifted — having fought for democracy abroad, they were no longer willing to accept second-class status at home.

Key Fact

Around 1 million Black Americans served in the Second World War in segregated units. The Double V Campaign (1942) demanded victory against fascism abroad AND discrimination at home. President Truman desegregated the armed forces by executive order in 1948 — a major early civil rights victory.

The Issue of Education: Brown v Board of Education, 1954

In 1896, the Supreme Court’s ruling in Plessy v Ferguson had established the doctrine of “separate but equal” — that segregated facilities were constitutional as long as they were equivalent in quality. In practice, Black schools received far less funding, had older buildings and fewer resources than white schools. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) mounted a legal challenge through the case of Oliver Brown, a parent in Topeka, Kansas.

On 17 May 1954, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Brown v Board of Education of Topeka that racially segregated schools were inherently unequal and therefore unconstitutional. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that segregation generated “a feeling of inferiority” in Black children that harmed their educational development. The ruling was a landmark: it directly challenged the legal foundations of segregation. However, white resistance in the South was fierce — 101 Southern congressmen signed the “Southern Manifesto” in 1956 pledging to resist.

The challenge of desegregating schools became national news in September 1957 when nine Black students — the “Little Rock Nine” — attempted to enrol at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Governor Orval Faubus called out the National Guard to block their entry. President Eisenhower, reluctant to intervene, eventually sent in 1,200 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students safely past jeering crowds. Television broadcast the confrontation to millions of Americans and to the world — making the reality of Southern segregation impossible to ignore.

Emmett Till, 1955

In August 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black teenager from Chicago, was visiting relatives in Money, Mississippi. He was abducted, brutally murdered and his body thrown into a river by two white men, Roy Bryant and J. W. Milam, following an alleged interaction with Bryant’s wife at a grocery store. The two men were acquitted by an all-white jury after deliberating for just 67 minutes. Till’s mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of Till’s body published in Jet magazine shocked the country and galvanised the civil rights movement.

Key Fact

Emmett Till was murdered in Mississippi in August 1955. His killers were acquitted by an all-white jury. His mother’s decision to hold an open-casket funeral and allow photographs of his body to be published brought the brutal reality of racial violence to national and international attention, energising the civil rights movement.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott, 1955–1956

On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks, a Black seamstress and NAACP activist in Montgomery, Alabama, refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a city bus — as required by local segregation ordinances. She was arrested. Local civil rights leaders, including the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., organised a boycott of the bus system. For 381 days, the vast majority of Black Montgomerians walked, cycled or carpooled rather than use the buses. The city’s bus company, which relied on Black passengers for around 70 per cent of its revenue, suffered serious financial losses.

In November 1956, the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v Gayle that bus segregation in Montgomery was unconstitutional. The boycott ended in December 1956 with the buses desegregated. The significance went far beyond Montgomery: it demonstrated that organised, disciplined, non-violent mass protest could succeed; it launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure; and it provided a model of protest that would be replicated across the South. The Montgomery Improvement Association, which led the boycott, evolved into the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC).
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark “Explain Significance” questions, always cover significance at the time AND over time. For the Montgomery Bus Boycott: significance at the time (desegregated buses, proved non-violent protest works, launched King) AND over time (model for sit-ins, Freedom Rides, later marches). For source-based questions about the civil rights movement, remember that sources from the 1950s South will often reflect white Southern perspectives — use your contextual knowledge to assess how useful and reliable they are.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Around 1 million Black Americans served in segregated units in the Second World War. The Double V Campaign (1942) linked the fight against fascism abroad to the fight against discrimination at home. Truman desegregated the military in 1948.
  • The Supreme Court’s Brown v Board of Education ruling (1954) declared school segregation unconstitutional, overturning the “separate but equal” doctrine. White resistance remained fierce — shown at Little Rock in 1957.
  • The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) showed that non-violent mass protest could force legal change, desegregated the city’s buses after 381 days, and launched Martin Luther King Jr. as the movement’s leading voice.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Double V Campaign launched by African Americans in 1942.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the feature (demanded victory against fascism abroad AND racial discrimination at home) AND develops it (popularised by the Pittsburgh Courier; showed Black Americans linked wartime service to demands for equality). Developing: Identifies feature without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-1956).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It lasted 381 days and involved the vast majority of Black Montgomerians refusing to use the buses, walking or carpooling instead; (2) It was organised using non-violent tactics by the Montgomery Improvement Association and established Martin Luther King Jr. as a civil rights leader. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v Board of Education (1954).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (NAACP legal campaign; the obvious inequality between Black and white schools; growing post-war pressure for civil rights reform) AND explains through a developed chain of reasoning how this cause led to the ruling. Secure: Cause with some development. Developing: Simple statement. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the murder of Emmett Till in 1955.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (energised civil rights movement; brought racial violence to national attention through open-casket funeral photographs; demonstrated inadequacy of Southern justice for Black Americans) AND explains the chain of effects with development. Secure: Consequence with some development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Brown v Board of Education ruling (1954) for the civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (struck down legal basis for school segregation; overturned Plessy v Ferguson; gave NAACP powerful legal precedent) AND over time (inspired further legal challenges; provoked white resistance that radicalised movement; Little Rock crisis showed limits of legal change without enforcement). Secure: One time frame covered well. Developing: Describes Brown without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important factor in advancing civil rights before 1955 was the legal strategy of the NAACP.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing NAACP legal strategy (Brown v Board; Browder v Gayle) against other factors (wartime service and Double V Campaign; Truman's 1948 executive order desegregating the army; grassroots protest demonstrated by Montgomery). Substantiated overall judgement on relative importance. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes NAACP without weighing against other factors. Emerging: Narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Double V Campaign demand?
options: Victory in the Pacific War only
Victory against fascism abroad AND discrimination at home
Votes for Black Americans in Southern states
Desegregation of the US army by 1943

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Supreme Court rule in Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
options: Segregated schools were constitutional if equally funded
Racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional
The GI Bill must be applied equally to Black veterans

knowledge_checks.q: The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted _____ days before the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.
Rosa Parks was arrested in December 1955 for refusing to give up her _____ on a Montgomery city bus.
Match each name to their significance in this period:
right: Chief Justice who wrote the Brown v Board ruling
Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
Baptist minister who led the bus boycott and became a national civil rights figure

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Double V Campaign (1942)?
flashcard_questions.a: A campaign demanding victory against fascism abroad and racial discrimination at home.

flashcard_questions.q: When did President Truman desegregate the US armed forces?
What did Brown v Board of Education (1954) rule?
flashcard_questions.a: That racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
The 'separate but equal' doctrine from Plessy v Ferguson (1896).

flashcard_questions.q: What happened at Little Rock, Arkansas in 1957?
flashcard_questions.a: President Eisenhower sent paratroopers to escort nine Black students into a desegregated school.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Emmett Till murdered and where?
Why was Emmett Till's murder significant for the civil rights movement?
flashcard_questions.a: His mother's open-casket funeral and published photographs of his body shocked the nation and galvanised activists.

flashcard_questions.q: Who refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery in December 1955?
How long did the Montgomery Bus Boycott last?
What was the outcome of the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
flashcard_questions.a: The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional; Montgomery's buses were desegregated.

flashcard_questions.q: Which organisation evolved from the Montgomery Improvement Association?
What were the Jim Crow laws?
flashcard_questions.a: Laws enforcing racial segregation in schools, transport and public spaces, mainly in the American South.

glossary_terms.definition: Laws and customs in the American South that enforced racial segregation in schools, transport, restaurants and public spaces.
A wartime campaign by African Americans demanding victory against fascism abroad AND against racial discrimination at home, symbolised by the letter V.

glossary_terms.definition: The 1954 Supreme Court ruling that declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional, overturning the 'separate but equal' doctrine of 1896.
